newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone hikes fuel prices to meet IMF demand.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone hikes fuel prices to meet IMF demand.

text.p: Sierra Leone hiked prices of petroleum products, including commonly-used kerosene, by up to 20 percent on Sunday to meet International Monetary Fund conditions for assistance, state radio said.

"The IMF made it clear that if the government failed to meet its demand immediately it would withdraw its assistance to the country," the Finance Ministry's financial secretray, Samura Kamara, said on the radio.

He added that if the hikes did not take place Sierra Leone would have compromised its case at a March 20 donors conference in Paris on international assistance for reconstruction and rehabilitation programmes in the West African country after five years of civil war.
The government had earlier refused to comply, citing the impact on the people of the impoverished state.
The IMF, keen to cut Sierra Leone's budget deficit, linked an increase in fuel prices to continued funding.
The budget deficit stands at more than $6 million.

A government statement carried by the radio said the pump price of premium grade petrol would go to 3,000 leones ($3.33) per litre from 2,500 leones. Kerosene goes to 2,000 leones from 1,700 leones while a litre of diesel would go to 2,600 from 2,000 leones.
The increase goes into effect immediately.
On Saturday officials said Sierra Leone had agreed to raise fuel prices at the IMF's request but had managed to persuade it to drop a demand that it also increase kerosene tariffs.
There was no immediate explanation for the inclusion of kerosene.
Officials sources said an IMF and World Bank team would visit Sierra Leone on March 27 to discuss future funding.
IMF officials in Sierra Leone were not immediately available for comment.
State radio, meanwhile, reported that President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah was leaving on Saturday for a three-day visit to Kuwait to strengthen ties between the two nations.

Sierra Leone is struggling to emerge from five years of civil war. Tejan Kabbah, who took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule, signed a peace deal with rebels in November. Implementation has dragged.
